items.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
items.summary_1line: vLLM announces day-0 support for Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini, a looped multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark, plus a Docker image.

items.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
items.summary_1line: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with about 26B total and 3B active parameters per token, using a looped transformer design and a 1M-token context.

items.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
items.summary_1line: An agent-driven tuning run on one RTX PRO 6000 raised single-user decode for Inkling 2 Mini from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) and 8-user aggregate throughput from about 570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) across 46 valid runs.

items.title: Show HN: Rust agent with an Inkling 2 Mini inference engine for Apple Silicon
items.summary_1line: Rustling is a Rust local inference engine for Inkling 2 Mini on Apple silicon that serves an OpenAI-compatible API for coding agents and includes a terminal chat that runs the model in-process with read, grep and glob tools.

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose topic cluster, not one event: three unrelated items about running inference on GPUs. Its main thread is AWS adding ways to share one GPU, starting with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU partitions for SageMaker endpoints on Nov 6.
prior_narrative.whats_new: AWS Lambda now runs GPU inference on EC2 G-series instances through Lambda Managed Instances, with up to 48 concurrent invocations sharing one model per GPU and vLLM/SGLang base images.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Two AWS launches in three weeks move GPU sharing into managed services, so small or bursty models no longer need a dedicated, mostly idle GPU endpoint.

open_questions: Which G-series instance types and regions does Lambda GPU support at launch?

prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you run small or bursty models on dedicated GPU endpoints, benchmark the same model on a SageMaker MIG partition and on Lambda GPU before your next capacity renewal.

prior_narrative.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research papers grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Nov 4 it ran through agent benchmarks, kernel and serving work, eval validity and multimodal hallucination, then Nov 13-19 papers on abstention, jailbreak screening and lie probes.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 23: ToolSmith has multimodal search agents generate and reuse their own tools across 13 benchmarks, three days after Search-RSI reported 9.8- and 9.5-point gains at 9B and 27B by growing the agent's search world.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the late-November run moves toward agents that extend their own tools, search space and memory, which touches tool registries and KV-cache budgets in a serving stack.

beats.summary: Multilingual tool use, long-term exploration memory, multimodal web agents and agents that zoom into high-resolution evidence.

beats.headline: Agent memory and knowledge engineering
beats.summary: What coding agents write down between tasks, agents that build taxonomies and knowledge bases, and a cached-memory architecture for 1M context.

beats.headline: Preference optimization and RLVR variants: debate, steerable adapters, token reweighting, populations
Updating what models know: unlearning, knowledge editing and false corrections
What do scores measure? Rater drift, framing, single runs and adaptive users
beats.summary: Chatbot Arena standards rising, one-run results on data-science tasks, recall evals that lean on entity names, and user simulators that may not track real users.

beats.headline: Multimodal hallucination: alignment and decoding fixes, then a check on how they are scored
beats.summary: Nov 23's CONCOR benchmark questions how contrastive decoding fixes have been evaluated.

beats.headline: Applied one-offs: federated learning, AutoML, diagnostics, anomaly detection and UX attribution
beats.summary: Grouped by shared wording, not by a common thread.

beats.headline: Serving-time safeguards: abstention, escalation, jailbreak screening and lie probes

beats.headline: Multimodal search agents that grow their own search worlds and tools
beats.summary: Search-RSI (Nov 20) expands the retrieval world as the agent improves; ToolSmith (Nov 23) generates and reuses new tools on a lean base library.

open_questions: Do ToolSmith's generated tools stay correct when reused on new tasks, and how is a faulty generated tool detected and retired?
Does MemOnce's 6.9x lower prefill at 1M context hold answer quality on long-context tasks beyond Qwen3.5-4B?
Do the knowledge and persona lie-probe directions detect lies on models outside the study, and at what false-positive rate?
Does the contrastive-prototype jailbreak detector report false-positive rates on benign prompts and hold up against adaptive attacks?
Does stability-compensated threshold calibration keep its error guarantee when the deployed model or prompt distribution shifts?
Under the CONCOR benchmark, which published contrastive decoding methods still reduce multimodal hallucination?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before letting an agent add tools or memory at runtime, gate it: review generated tools before they enter the shared registry, log which ones get reused, and measure any cached-memory scheme's answer quality on your own long-context traffic, not only its prefill latency.

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of arXiv papers proposing new agent benchmarks, starting with multi-agent decision and coordination tests (TandemBench, WorkflowArena). Later papers moved to MCP hallucination, memory poisoning, and long-horizon real-world tasks such as AI infra tuning and research sessions.
prior_narrative.whats_new: REPA (Nov 23) models how one agent's local errors propagate into system-level failures across multi-agent workflows, two days after MASSys showed Star vs Chain topology rankings flip under KV-cache pressure.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Multi-agent scores now depend on serving substrate and error propagation, not just the model, so a leaderboard number may not hold on your own inference stack.

beats.headline: Benchmarks target how agents divide work and coordinate
beats.summary: Decision models, workflow orchestration, shared-memory coordination, and full-duplex voice task handling each get a dedicated test.

beats.headline: Tool calls, memory, and multi-turn state come under test
beats.summary: MCP hallucinations, memory poisoning across sessions, and user-state tracking over turns; two memory papers sit at the theme's edge.

beats.headline: Long-horizon, real-world task benchmarks multiply
beats.summary: AI infra optimization, live research workspaces, privacy-aware code review, multi-arm robot control, video, and spatial exploration.

beats.headline: The system layer: serving substrate and error propagation
beats.summary: Papers now measure what happens around the agents: batch scheduling, serving load, and how local errors cascade.

open_questions: Does MASSys's topology-ranking flip under KV-cache pressure reproduce on other serving stacks?
Does REPA's error-propagation model hold beyond the three Qwen base models it was evaluated on?

storylines.label: Weight-Space Programming
storylines.latest_title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?

prior_narrative.tldr: An MIT report that a frontier LLM can write and read small neural network weights in a single reply set off a run of follow-ups in mid-November: an open-source instruction set (W-ISA), a game-agent compilation paper, and an independent replication. A Nov 18 paper then moved from capability edits to value edits, and a Nov 23 CLIP paper borrowed the name for a closed-form weight-editing recipe.
prior_narrative.whats_new: MBZUAI researchers report Claude Opus 5.5 solved only 26% of hard mazes directly, but a transformer it wrote by setting weights solved 100% of their test mazes in 39 minutes for $19, with no training run.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: If an LLM can hand-author a small model that beats its own direct answers, weight-writing becomes a cheap way to build narrow task solvers, and an untracked way to change a model's behavior.

beats.headline: W-ISA proposes an instruction set for programming LLM weights
Papers compile game rules into agents and reproduce the core claim
beats.summary: One paper tests whether compiled game agents generalize to held-out levels; another reproduces the MIT write-weights and read-weights results.

beats.headline: Weight edits aimed at ethical priorities and CLIP retrieval
beats.summary: A value-edit study on a concept-supervised text model and a closed-form CLIP recipe reported across 21 checkpoints; the CLIP work shares the name more than the LLM-authored method.

beats.headline: LLM-written transformer solves all test mazes for $19
beats.summary: Looped weight-space programming beats the same model's direct answers, 100% versus 26% on hard mazes.

open_questions: Does weight-space programming work beyond small networks, on production-scale LLM layers?
Does the MBZUAI maze result hold on tasks other than mazes, and has anyone reproduced it?
Can weight-space edits be detected by inspecting a served checkpoint?
Does W-ISA gain adoption or a reference implementation from a major lab?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Treat LLM-written weights as a research option for narrow, verifiable tasks only. Add checkpoint hashing and behavior regression evals now, since direct weight edits leave no training trail.

storylines.label: Cache Serving
storylines.latest_title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose theme thread, not one event: 22 independent items from Nov 6 to Nov 24 that each cut inference or agent cost at a different layer, mostly arXiv papers plus posts from Google, Baseten, Microsoft Research, UW, AWS and vLLM. Through Nov 19 the KV cache was the most-attacked target, ending with RoCoKV and TideCache.
prior_narrative.whats_new: vLLM shipped vLLM-GR on Nov 24, an open-source serving framework that adds beam search over semantic item IDs so generative recommendation models such as OneRec can run on the vLLM stack.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: KV-cache memory is still the most-attacked bottleneck here (6 of 22 items), and vLLM-GR shows mainstream serving engines now stretching to non-chat workloads, so one serving stack may soon cover both LLM and recommendation traffic.

beats.headline: Serving stacks: XLA Serving Engine, edge simulation, cross-Region routing
beats.summary: Infrastructure that decides where and on what hardware requests run.

beats.headline: Cheaper decoding: draft pruning, diffusion blocks, MoE traffic, small models
beats.summary: Efficiency inside the model and decode loop: cheaper draft verification, overlapping diffusion blocks, less all-to-all traffic, quantization and a 4GB agent model.

beats.headline: Shrink what the model reads and writes: images, audio, chain-of-thought
beats.summary: Token reduction on input (VLM cropping, chunked long-audio ASR) and on output (shorter chain-of-thought training targets).

beats.headline: Agent-level efficiency: coordinated delegation and learned token budgets
beats.summary: Cost cuts at the agent layer rather than the serving stack.

beats.headline: The KV cache becomes the main target
beats.summary: Six papers attack cache memory: intent-aware prefix reuse, verified compression, prefill/decode KV translation, Gemma 4 shared K=V storage, reasoning-trace compression, and hybrid-model cache streaming in SGLang.

beats.headline: Keyword matches outside LLM serving
beats.summary: Two papers share the word "efficient" but address robot-policy RL training and an answer-evidence classifier, not inference serving.

beats.headline: vLLM extends to generative recommendation with vLLM-GR
beats.summary: A mainstream serving engine adds a non-chat decoding mode: beam search over semantic item IDs.

open_questions: Do any of the KV-cache methods (RoCoKV, Verify Before You Fetch, BridgeKV) land in vLLM, SGLang or another mainstream serving engine?
Does TideCache's SGLang implementation get merged upstream or released as code?
Does the Gemma 4 store-K=V-once trick ship in a paged serving engine release, and with what measured memory savings?
Does Google publish throughput or latency benchmarks for XLA Serving Engine against vLLM on the same hardware?
Does vLLM-GR report throughput numbers against existing recommendation serving stacks?
Does TokenEconomizer report a token or cost reduction on a public coding-agent benchmark?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If long-context or reasoning workloads are memory-bound, profile KV-cache size per request before buying GPUs; if you run generative recommendation on a separate stack, test vLLM-GR before building custom beam-search serving.
